claim: LangSmith ships a validated prompt by moving a named 'environment' pointer (Staging or Production) onto an already-versioned, immutable commit -- promotion never rewrites the prompt, only where the pointer points -- and rollback works the same way: each environment keeps its own ordered history of past pointer values, so a rollback is just re-pointing to an earlier commit from that recorded history, not restoring content from a backup.
query: LangSmith prompt hub deployment promote production version
read: Environments represent named deployment targets, Staging and Production, that you can assign to specific commits. They let you track which version of a prompt is active in each environment and promote commits between them. ... Promoting a commit to Production does not remove it from Staging. ... Roll back an environment Each environment maintains an ordered history of which commits were assigned to it and when. To roll back to a previous commit: In the left pane, find the environment you want to roll back. Click the rollback icon for that environment. From the displayed Rollback history, select the commit you want to roll back to. The environment pointer will update to that commit.

read: Start with shadow deployments. Run your new configuration alongside the existing one without serving results to users. ... Deploy to internal users who can provide detailed feedback. Then expand to beta testers who represent your target audience. Next, roll out to a small percentage of production traffic (typically starting at 5-10%). Finally, monitor metrics carefully and increase rollout percentage if everything remains stable. Keep your configurations versioned and documented. Include metadata like version numbers, update dates, and change descriptions in your configurations. This creates an audit trail and makes it easier to track which changes led to which outcomes. Implement fallback configurations. If your primary model provider has issues or if a new configuration isn't performing well, you need a proven, stable configuration to fall back on. These fallbacks should be simple and reliable.

claim: Two concrete differences from an ordinary-code canary are named: (1) the exposed unit is route/tenant/intent-scoped rather than a whole service instance -- '1% of billing-support prompts, a single enterprise tenant, or only low-risk intents' -- because a wrong early agent decision (e.g. tool choice) cascades through several downstream steps rather than failing cleanly; and (2) because the canary response is live to real users (not mirrored), the rollback threshold must be made explicit before traffic is shifted at all, not decided after seeing a bad outcome.
query: agent behavior rollback feature flag canary deployment LLM 2026
read: Canary deployment for LLMs is an LLM-gateway release pattern that sends a small, controlled share of real production traffic to a new model, prompt, router, or guardrail before wider rollout. Unlike traffic mirroring, the canary response is returned to real users, so quality gates must watch latency, cost, error rate, safety, and task outcome by cohort. ... A candidate model that chooses a different first tool can cascade into wrong state, stale context, or an expensive loop three steps later. Unlike blue-green deployment, where the whole environment swaps, an LLM canary often needs route-level control: 1% of billing-support prompts, a single enterprise tenant, or only low-risk intents. Unlike traffic mirroring, a canary is live exposure, so it needs faster detection and tighter rollback.
snippet: Canary deployment for LLMs is an LLM-gateway release pattern that sends a small, controlled share of real production traffic to a new model, prompt, router, or guardrail before wider rollout.
title: What Is Canary Deployment? LLM Gateway Guide (2026)
topic: Canary deployment applied to an LLM/agent change specifically: route-scoped exposure and an explicit pre-declared rollback threshold

claim: Caveat first: this is a not-yet-peer-reviewed arXiv preprint (id 2605.28097 places it in arXiv's May-2026 submission batch, YYMM naming, within this repo's six-month window) about canarying safety-critical embodied (physical/robotic) agents -- it proposes a construction, it is not a report of observed production practice, so it answers Q3/Q2 as a design idea rather than as evidence of what shipped platforms actually do. The idea itself: a crash during a canary (an exception from the metrics provider, a policy-hook bug, a network partition) is treated as a failure mode distinct from an ordinary end-of-window rollback, because a naive implementation can mark the job failed while leaving the provisional (candidate) version active even though the canary has terminated -- so the fix wraps the canary body in a try/except that runs the rollback closure before re-raising, precisely so a crash cannot leave a promoted-looking candidate silently serving.

read: The challenging case is a crash during the canary: the metrics provider raises an exception, a bug in a policy hook fires, or a network partition severs the bridge from the executor. ... leaving the provisional version active even though the canary has terminated. ... Our integration adds a try / except around the canary body that calls the rollback closure before re-raising
snippet: The construction is symmetric with respect to failure: when a canary rolls back at the end of the soak window

claim: Same caveat as record 008: this is an arXiv preprint (2605.28097, May-2026 batch by arXiv's YYMM id convention) in the specific domain of AEROS-governed embodied (physical/robotic) agents, whose unit of promotion is an 'Embodied Capability Module' (ECM) -- not a general claim about LLM/chat agents, and not a report of shipped practice. What its own read text establishes: AEROS already ships a governed-evolution pipeline for promoting an ECM update through a 'validator / sandbox / shadow / rollback sequence' -- i.e. a named, multi-gate promotion pipeline is treated as existing baseline practice in this domain. The paper's own concern is that a naive percentage-rollout canary on top of that pipeline can still break agent identity: 'episodic memory entries written before, during, and after the canary refer to different identity hashes,' which forces per-event identity resolution in the audit chain and makes full re-certification 'the safest practice, and prohibitive' at scale. Whether this identity-entanglement concern applies to a non-embodied LLM/prompt-routing agent is not established by this source and would need its own record.
